Household spending remains flat: ABS
Household spending was unchanged in August, according to new Australian Bureau of Statistics data, but excluding fuel spending, total household spending would have fallen by 0.3 per cent.
It said the household spending numbers for the month of August was flat after rising in both July (+1.1 per cent) and June (+0.9 per cent).
Household spending was 6.8 per cent higher than the same time last year.
ABS head of business statistics Tom Lay said recreation and culture spending saw the largest fall — down 1.4 per cent — after months of higher spending associated with major sporting events.

"Clothing and footwear, Recreational goods, Food, Health, and Furniture also fell," he said."These falls were offset by higher transport spending — up 2.3 per cent — leaving overall household spending unchanged from July.""Both fuel spending and new vehicle sales contributed to this rise, especially electric vehicles sales as households respond to rising fuel prices."
"Clothing and footwear, Recreational goods, Food, Health, and Furniture also fell," he said.
"These falls were offset by higher transport spending — up 2.3 per cent — leaving overall household spending unchanged from July."
"Both fuel spending and new vehicle sales contributed to this rise, especially electric vehicles sales as households respond to rising fuel prices."
Fuel spending rose 8.1 per cent in August, following the full restoration of the fuel excise duty from August 3.
The Federal Government cut the fuel excise tax on April 1 to help families struggling with high global oil prices.
The discount dropped to a partial 16 cents a litre in July and relief ended entirely on August 3, returning the full excise rate to 53.7 cents a litre.
The ABS said excluding fuel spending, total household spending would have fallen by 0.3 per cent.
Experimental data produced by the ABS suggests that the volume of fuel spending fell by 0.5 per cent in August. This follows a 4.6 per cent decrease in July.
Employers grow more cautious on hiring
Australian workers are increasingly staying in their jobs, as employers also become more cautious about growing their workforces.
And workplace grievances and complaints are rising, according to new Australian HR Institute (AHRI) research.

Its Q3 2026 Australian Work Outlook report found that employer wage increase expectations have risen from 3.1 per cent to 3.4 per cent, putting greater pressure on organisations' capacity to provide a wage premium for managers.
Employment confidence fell to its equal-lowest level since 2023, while average annual employee turnover remained near the survey's historic lows at 13.4 per cent, down from 15.2 per cent in 2025.

These findings align with Australian Bureau of Statistics data showing 7.2 per cent of employed Australians changed employer or business in the year to February 2026, down from 7.7 per cent the previous year.
AHRI found 21 per cent of employers expect redundancies, up from 19 per cent, although this remains below the survey's historical average.
In the workplace, grievances and complaints are rising, with 32 per cent of employers reporting an increase this year.
AHRI said persistently low job mobility also presents challenges for employers seeking to attract experienced talent.
"Workers are staying put and employers are thinking harder about every new hire," AHRI chief executive Sarah McCann-Bartlett said.

"That creates stability, but it also creates a risk that organisations become too static at a time when they need new skills, fresh thinking and greater productivity."For employers, the challenge is no longer simply how to retain people, but how to make sure a more stable workforce continues to develop, perform and adapt."

Anthropic's IPO prospectus shows sweeping AI vision, surging costs
Anthropic is making a massive bet that AI will transform the global economy more profoundly than industrialisation, electricity and the internet, according to its IPO prospectus.
But the cost to get there will be staggering.

Anthropic reported a net loss of $US42 billion ($59.9 billion) in 2025, and plans to spend $US518 billion on cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations in the coming years, according to the prospectus seen by Reuters.
The prospectus also details how the company has grown sharply in the last year — while also posting wider losses.

Revenue grew 12-fold in 2025 to nearly $US4.6 billion, even as the company lost more than $US8 billion on an operating basis, excluding write-downs of various liabilities mostly tied to previous fundraising, according to the documents.

The public sale, which could value it at more than $US2 trillion, would capitalise on the rapid rise of the AI startup lab that only came into existence five years ago, and establish it as a benchmark for how Wall Street values AI's leading companies, including rival OpenAI.

The plans come as Anthropic confronts evidence from its own research that increasingly autonomous AI models can behave in unexpected and potentially harmful ways, including sabotaging code, assisting fraud and manipulating information in controlled tests.
These reports have broken into the wider public sphere, igniting fears about how companies can keep increasingly powerful systems under control as they race to deploy them commercially.
Anthropic's debut would follow SpaceX's blockbuster IPO that valued Elon Musk's company at $US1.77 trillion.
Reporting with Reuters

Senior Economist at realestate.com.auEleanor Creagh, says an increase will put "further pressure on household budgets".

"Higher mortgage repayments will weigh on discretionary spending at a time when households are already contending with elevated living costs, although resilient employment and incomes continue to provide an important buffer," she says.

"For the housing market, another rate rise reinforces the downturn already underway. Higher mortgage rates further reduce borrowing capacities and buyer budgets, adding to the downward pressure on home prices and sales activity."
Creagh says, however, this remains an "orderly adjustment" rather than a "distressed housing correction".
"Labour market conditions remain relatively resilient, very few borrowers are in negative equity, while many households retain substantial repayment buffers," she says.
"The RBA does not target home prices, and the current housing slowdown is one of the channels through which tighter monetary policy is working to reduce demand.

"While structural housing undersupply remains a long-term support for prices, in the near-term, affordability constraints, higher borrowing costs and weaker buyer demand are likely to keep downward pressure on prices."

Another RBA rate rise could push home ownership further out of reach, according to one expert
An interest rate hike today could further reduce borrowing capacity, making home ownership harder to achieve for many Australians, according to Domain's Chief Residential Economist, Dr Nicola Powell.

"Every increase in interest rates reduces the amount buyers can borrow, limiting what they can afford to pay and pushing some aspiring homeowners out of the market altogether," she says."For many, that means delaying their plans while they save a larger deposit or work to meet stricter lending requirements."
"Every increase in interest rates reduces the amount buyers can borrow, limiting what they can afford to pay and pushing some aspiring homeowners out of the market altogether," she says.
"For many, that means delaying their plans while they save a larger deposit or work to meet stricter lending requirements."

Higher interest rates may also slow the delivery of new housing as building approvals remain subdued, and residential construction is increasingly competing with major infrastructure, renewable energy and data-centre projects for the same labour and materials.
All of this, according to Dr Powell, makes it harder and more costly to bring new homes to market.
"The bigger challenge is what higher rates could mean for future housing supply," she says.

"Australia's construction industry only has so much capacity. As labour and materials are drawn into other major projects, it becomes harder and more expensive to bring new housing developments to market.

"The risk is that today's fight against inflation becomes tomorrow's housing shortage. Higher rates may help cool demand in the short term, but they can also make it harder to increase housing supply and address Australia's long-term housing shortfall."

A hike by the RBA is needed to 'maintain credibility', according to one analyst
In order to maintain credibility, the RBA will have to hike today, according to RBC BlueBay Asset Management's Malin Rosengren.
"They held rates unchanged in August on the concession that if any upside risks to inflation materialise verse their expectations, they will have to respond," she says.
July inflation data indicates both headline and trimmed-mean inflation remain elevated, and while the labour market loosened modestly, Rosengren says it doesn’t seem enough to soften demand.

"At this point it should appear evident to the RBA that policy is not yet restrictive enough. If they fail to hike at the September meeting, the market will turn to price in more inflation premia across the curve as the bank’s credibility will be tarnished," she says.

"A September hike will make another tightening step in November near unavoidable. The November meeting will include updated economic forecasts, where projections for inflation and growth are sure to be lifted over the horizon & suggest further tightening is required."
On the positive, Rosengren says two more hikes to a policy rate of 4.85% should be restrictive enough to "get the job done" for the RBA.

"Tightening will increasingly feed into the real economy, working with a significant lag, and eventually become more material in the data (though of course much depends on energy prices and the external environment)," she says.

Wall St close indicates fresh pressure on yields, according to one analyst
All major US exchanges on Wall Street closed down on Monday afternoon.
• The S&P 500 closed down -0.8% to 7,684 points.
• The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down -0.7% to 51,482 points.
• The Nasdaq closed down -1.1% to 30,277 points.

Senior financial market analyst at capital.com Kyle Rodda says Wall Street's "dip" came after last week's "very modest peace premium in energy markets", which has put "fresh upward pressure on yields and downward pressure on stocks and non-yielding assets like precious metals".

"Geopolitical developments remain very headline-driven and revolve around the prospect of a peace deal. The situation has reverted to the familiar he-said-she-said funny business where a trial balloon floated by one side is promptly rejected by the other, with the side that purportedly floated it denying they did so in the first place," he says.

"However, behind the rhetoric there appears to be some shift in power dynamics underpinning negotiations. The Iranians seem to be increasingly losing leverage as they lose control of the Strait of Hormuz and the isolation tactics by the US put a squeeze on their economy.

"Some energy analysts suggest oil flows out of the Persian Gulf have reverted to more than 90% of their pre-war levels, potentially explaining Iran’s stronger motivation to make a deal and the Trump administration’s stubbornness and reluctance to compromise."
As for Australia and interest rates, Rodda says "Futures imply a roughly 93% chance of a rate hike from the central bank as it struggles to contain above-target inflation".

"While it has pulled the rug from underneath the markets before, it appears unlikely the RBA will defy market pricing and leave rates unchanged," he says."Instead, the more likely source of volatility will come as the markets assess the central bank’s language regarding the risk of further hikes to come."At present, the markets ascribe that a roughly 67% chance."

Rate hikes leave borrowers hundreds of dollars poorer
A 25-basis-point increase in the cash rate would add $91 a month on a typical $600,000 mortgage, said Sally Tindall, data insights director at financial comparison site Canstar.

"The true pain is in the cumulative impact,'' she said."Across what is likely to be at least four rate rises for the year, this borrower has to fork out an extra $364 a month compared to what they were paying at the start of the year."
"The true pain is in the cumulative impact,'' she said.
"Across what is likely to be at least four rate rises for the year, this borrower has to fork out an extra $364 a month compared to what they were paying at the start of the year."

The difference since October 2011 - the last time rates were that high - is that soaring house prices have resulted in home loan debt rising from $1.05 trillion to $2.51 trillion over the same period, Ms Tindall said.
Mortgage holders are set to shoulder hundreds of dollars more in monthly repayments compared to the start of the year, with interest rates expected to hit a 15-year high.
At 4.6%, the cash rate is set to be the highest experienced by a generation of borrowers.
That will lift the average owner-occupier variable rate to 6.49%, assuming the increase is fully passed on by lenders, which they usually are.

With the Middle East conflict and the artificial intelligence boom pushing up prices for commodities and technology components respectively, the Reserve Bank board has seemingly lost patience and is willing to inflict greater costs on the economy and unemployment to get inflation down.

Comments by RBA governor Michele Bullock that unemployment needed to be between 4.5 and 5.0% to help get inflation back under control were met with a furious response from union groups and the social service sector.
"Raising interest rates is creating unemployment by design, putting thousands of people out of work to slow the economy," Australian Council of Social Service chief executive Cassandra Goldie said.
"Since interest rates started to increase, an extra 200,000 people are out of paid work.
"Increasing unemployment towards five per cent would cause a human disaster, locking people out of paid work for years and forcing them to rely on grossly inadequate income support payments."
Treasurer Jim Chalmers also pushed back on Ms Bullock's comments.
"What we have seen is that it's possible in this country to have lower unemployment than (five per cent) at the same time as inflation comes off," he told reporters on Monday.
"We have an inflation challenge in our economy not because unemployment is too low but because the price of petrol is too high and we've got other inflationary pressures in our economy.
"I'm reluctant to blame the workers of this country for our inflation challenge."
- Reporting by AAP

Chalmers defends taxation as a percentage of GPD
Chalmers defends taxing, spending as a percentage of GDP
Jim Chalmers has again defended the level of government taxation, which is expected to tick up according to the latest forecasts.
Yesterday's Final Budget Update showed forecast tax receipts as a percentage of GDP jumped from May's forecast of 23.6 to 24.1.
That falls just under the 24.2 per cent number reached during the John Howard Coalition government.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Chalmers says tax receipts as a percentage of GDP is still lower than the Howard government.
"Well, it's still lower than what we saw under Howard and Costello, is the first point," Chalmers says.

"We're cutting taxes and there are more tax cuts already in the budget on the way. So we're cutting income taxes because we recognise that's a good way to help people with the cost of living. If we weren't doing that, tax to GDP would be higher."

Is there any chance of an interest rate hold today?
Independent economist Chris Richardson says the economy needs to take its metaphorical medicine to bring inflation down.
On the program last night, business presenter and correspondent David Taylor asked Richardson if there's any chance the RBA will defy odds and keep rates on hold today.
His answer was one word - "no".
"To bring inflation down, there has to be pain for someone," says Richardson.
Unfortunately, that pain will mainly lie with middle-income earners with mortgages.
"The most likely thing I would say is we get the rate rise ... I think if we get one [today] and then one more on Melbourne Cup day then we might avoid one more next year," says Richardson.
An interest rate hike today would take official cash rate to 15-year high
The Reserve Bank meets today for the sixth time this year, and financial markets and economists think it will almost certainly raise interest rates for the fourth time this year.
Another standard 25-basis-point rate hike would take the RBA's cash rate target from 4.35% to 4.6%, the highest level since the start of November 2011.

Treasurer still keen on tax cuts despite inflation challenge
It appears Treasurer Jim Chalmers remains committed to tax cuts despite sticky inflation pointing to an all-but-certain interest rate hike by the Reserve Bank of Australia today.
Speaking on the ABC's News Breakfast program this morning, Mr Chalmers said he understood the financial pressure Australians were under.

"It's why our cost-of-living relief is so important in the form of tax cuts and more bulk-billing and higher wages, help for first-home buyers in the housing market," he said."All of that recognises that Australians are under very substantial pressure and, obviously, if interest rates go up, that will add to the pressures that people are feeling."
"It's why our cost-of-living relief is so important in the form of tax cuts and more bulk-billing and higher wages, help for first-home buyers in the housing market," he said.
"All of that recognises that Australians are under very substantial pressure and, obviously, if interest rates go up, that will add to the pressures that people are feeling."

Tax cuts will likely send more cash into the economy and are in stark contrast to calls for the government to ease pressure on mortgage holders by pulling cash out of the economy through imposing new taxes, or even raising superannuation contributions.
Mr Chalmers instead defended the government's economic record.
"Spending as a share of GDP is much lower than when we came to office. We delivered a couple of surpluses. We've now got the deficit much lower.
"Public debt is a fraction of what we see in other countries.

"It's really important to remember that this inflation challenge in our economy has a number of sources. We do have an inflation challenge, which is made much, much worse by developments in the Middle East. It means Australians are already paying a very hefty price for developments on the other side of the world."
He also disputed suggestions that unemployment needed to rise to get inflation under control.

"It's not primarily the fault of Australian workers. We're seeing inflation in our economy for a range of reasons, including the war in the Middle East. It's possible to have full employment, low unemployment, at the same time as we have lower, more steady inflation. That's the Reserve Bank's objective, and it's the government's objective too."

See the bond yields rise
Government bond yields moved higher overnight, with higher oil prices driving the move.
According to NAB chief economist Sally Auld, the yield on the 30-year US Treasury bond is now 5.57 per cent, its highest level since 2004.
She said yield rises across the market were in the order of 8-9bps for US Treasuries, while moves in European markets were a little lower.

"The French 10-year government yields rose 8bps, while German 10-year yields were up 6bps, continuing the under-performance of French sovereign paper," she said."Ahead of the RBA, the implied yield on the AUS 10-year bond future was up 2bps, while the implied yield on the 3-year contract was up 0.5bp," she said.
